intrinsic_value_estimate: $74-86 per share (central case about $80). Method: capitalize core owner earnings on the assumption that the future looks like the past (brk-letter-1981#3, brk-letter-1986). Base core owner earnings of about $1.88 per share in 1987 (net income $916M + D&A $154M - undistributed equity income $80M - deferred tax $29M - maintenance capex of about $225M - affiliate dividends of $39M, over 372M shares). Grown at 11% for 10 years, matching the 1977-87 EPS record, then 4-5%, discounted at an assumed 9% long-Treasury rate. Affiliates (CPE, CCE, TCC, other) added at their $2.26B carrying value, about $6 per share. Conservative case (8% growth, 10% discount rate) gives $50. Franchise-weakens case (5%, 10%) gives $38. The stock fails the old net-working-capital test: NWC is about $0.05 per share against a $46.56 price.
margin_of_safety: At $46.56, the price is 37-46% below the $74-86 value on the 'future resembles the past' basis, which meets the framework's standard of a price substantially below value to a private owner. The margin is about 7% on the conservative case ($50) and negative in the franchise-weakens case ($38). The margin depends on the franchise staying durable, not on asset backing. Put another way, the price implies only about 3-7% annual growth in owner earnings against a 10-year record of about 11%.

key_reasons.reason: The core business earns very high returns on equity without needing leverage, which passes the framework's primary test.
key_reasons.framework_principle: 3. Return on equity, not EPS growth, is the primary test (brk-letter-1979)
key_reasons.evidence: ROE was 27.2% in 1987 and 28.8% in 1986 (about 25% excluding one-off items). With net debt of 15.3% of capital stripped out, the return on net capital is about 25%. ROE was 19.7-21.2% in 1976-80 with debt at only 3.5-9.3% of capital. Core return excluding the $2.26B of affiliate capital is above 50% (ar-1986, ar-1987).

key_reasons.reason: The franchise has a durable and widening moat that has survived a major management error.
key_reasons.framework_principle: 3. Durable competitive advantage: the moat around the castle (brk-letter-1986)
key_reasons.evidence: Over 44% of world soft-drink sales at twice the nearest competitor's volume. US share above 39% against the competitor's ~30%. Fountain share 59%, outselling the next rival more than 2 to 1. Self-described low-cost producer in most of 155 countries. US operating income rose 10% on 1% shipment growth through efficiency. Original formula returned as 'classic' after 1985 and became the No. 1 US soft drink (ar-1986, ar-1987).

key_reasons.reason: Owner earnings are high relative to the capital the business needs, which leaves cash for buybacks and growth.
key_reasons.evidence: 1987 capex was $300M (3.9% of revenue) against D&A of $154M. Owner earnings come to about $661-809M, or $1.78-2.17 per share. Shareholders received more than 100% of earnings in 1984-87 through dividends and buybacks (ar-1987).

key_reasons.reason: Retained earnings have produced well over $1 of market value per $1 retained, even after removing the market's re-rating of the stock.
key_reasons.framework_principle: 4. Each $1 retained must create at least $1 of market value (brk-letter-1983)
key_reasons.evidence: From 1982 to 1987, EPS totalled $10.97 and dividends $6.69 (including the $0.90 CPE in-kind dividend), so $4.28 per share was retained. Over the same period the share price rose from $11.58 to $38.13 (+$26.55, about 6x the amount retained), and to $46.56 by the as-of date. At the constant 1981 P/E the gain is still about 2.3x (ar-1987, prices).

key_reasons.reason: Management is in place and shareholder-oriented, with large buybacks made below today's price and a shift back to the core business.
key_reasons.framework_principle: 4. Management in place; buybacks only well below intrinsic value (brk-letter-1982, brk-letter-1984)
key_reasons.evidence: The team has been in place since 1981. It repurchased 18.4M shares at about $18 in 1984, 15M at about $25 in 1985 and 14.1M at about $43 in 1987, and has authorized up to 40M more shares (over 10% of the company) through 1990. It exited plastics and pasta, spun out entertainment, and says it is 'first and foremost a marketer of soft drinks' (>95% of operating income) (ar-1986, ar-1987).

key_reasons.reason: The price makes sense even if the future only resembles the past. The investor's later standard prefers an outstanding business at a sensible price over a bargain in a mediocre one.
key_reasons.framework_principle: 5. Valuation, read with brk-letter-1981#3 and brk-letter-1987#18 (outstanding business at a sensible price); the net-working-capital rule fails and is superseded
key_reasons.evidence: Price $46.56 is 19.2x 1987 EPS of $2.43. After removing about $6 per share of affiliates, the core trades at about 21.6x owner earnings, a 4.6% yield. That price implies only about 3-7% growth against about 11% EPS growth in 1977-87. Estimated value is $74-86 per share (prices, ar-1987).

key_reasons.reason: No catalyst is needed, the size can matter at Berkshire's scale, and the facts are clear enough to justify a concentrated position.
key_reasons.framework_principle: 6. No catalyst needed (brk-letter-1987); 7. Concentrate when the facts are clear (bpl-letter-1965); 1. Hunt elephants (brk-letter-1987)
key_reasons.evidence: Market value is $17.3B and net income $916M, so a $0.5-1B position is possible. Berkshire's three permanent holdings were worth about $2.1B at end-1987 (brk-letter-1987#18). Dividends have been raised 26 years in a row and are $1.20 for 1988 (ar-1987, prices).

risks: No 1988 results in the packet, so the 1987 base could be stale and current trends cannot be checked
Currency: about 74-77% of operating income is earned abroad. Currency added about 27% to 1986 and 16% to 1987 dollar results, and a stronger dollar would cut reported earnings
Capital allocation drift: $2.26B in affiliates earning about 5% against a stated 12% hurdle, and a past record of diversification paid for partly in stock
Leverage and off-balance-sheet exposure: gross debt is 45.6% of capital, about $719M of contingent guarantees and recourse, and CCE carries $2.72B of liabilities
Reporting is promotional and below the framework's standard of candor; insider ownership and pay levels are unknown
The price is near its 52-week high ($49.12) and well above the 1988 range of $35-40, so the margin of safety depends on the franchise lasting
Foods segment is weak and exposed to commodity orange-juice prices, though it is about 5% of operating income
Discount rate and maintenance capex are assumptions, not packet figures
what_would_change_my_mind: 1988 results showing local-currency soft-drink operating income growth falling well below the ~8% recent pace, or soft-drink margins falling
Evidence that 1988 buybacks were small or made only at high prices, or that the ~$1.2B of debt capacity is going to large acquisitions outside soft drinks
Market values or results of CCE/CPE showing the affiliates are worth well below carrying value, or that the parent is implicitly backing CCE's debt
Meeting management and finding they are not candid, or that insiders own little stock
Price rising to about $75-80 or more before the position is built, which would remove the margin of safety
Signs of lost pricing power, such as volume falling broadly after price increases or the concentrate gross margin dropping well below ~63%
sell_triggers: Lasting erosion of the moat: sustained world or US share loss to the primary competitor, or unlevered return on capital falling toward 15% or below
Management issues stock on terms unfavorable to owners or makes large diversifying acquisitions that repeat the entertainment mistake (brk-letter-1982#17)
The business starts to need debt to keep its returns up, for example net debt above the 35% ceiling to fund operations rather than buybacks
Evidence of accounting manipulation or a lack of candor about material business facts
A far better use of capital is clearly available AND the price is far above any reasonable estimate of intrinsic value (secondary; the default is to hold a great business permanently)
